title: The shelf
where: Auden’s reading list of 1941, and the books to read here
intro: A mimeographed reading list survives from the course. The standard bibliography of Auden, by Bloomfield and Mendelson, describes it as two sheets. Alan Jacobs, a scholar of Auden, published a picture of the first sheet in 2012 with the permission of Auden’s estate, and [it can be seen on his site](https://blog.ayjay.org/audensyllabus/).

The list is headed English 135, Fate and the Individual in European Literature. Under the title it gives the particulars: first semester, two hours of credit, Thursdays from four to six in 2215 Angell Hall, open to juniors, seniors and graduate students who have the written permission of Professor Arno Bader. The instructor’s name is typed as “W. Auden.” The list carries no year, and Bloomfield and Mendelson put it in the fall semester of 1941.

case.label: The required books and the libretti as spines, each as thick as its book is long
case.note: Each spine is as thick as its book is long in the copy printed here, at 350 words or 35 lines of verse to the page. The number on a spine is its pages by that count. The short spines are the opera libretti. Together the copies come to about 4,800 pages. A spine opens its book.

keys.absent: Not printed here, and not drawn to scale

required.title: Required reading
intro: The list has twenty-three entries of required reading. One entry offers a choice between *Agamemnon* and *Antigone*. On the published sheet someone has written “Omit” by hand beside two others, *Faust* and *The Education of Henry Adams*. Who wrote it is not recorded. That makes twenty-four works, and each has a page on this site.

opera.title: Opera libretti
intro: The list assigns nine opera libretti as reading. Donald Pearce, who took the course, remembers that Auden brought a phonograph and records to class.

The list names no editions of the libretti. Most of the texts printed here are the English versions from the bilingual libretti that Fred Rullman of New York published. Where an entry names no translator, the libretto names none. With each opera there is one old record, made between 1909 and 1924.

critical.title: Recommended criticism
intro: The list recommends eighteen books of criticism. None of them is printed here. Where one is out of copyright in the United States and this site found a free copy online, the entry links to it.

The first sheet ends after the eighth of them, so the published picture shows only those eight. The other ten are known from Charles Miller, who took the course and prints the list in his memoir. The list gets three of the authors’ names wrong, and Miller’s copy has slips of its own. This site corrects both kinds of error.

works.author: Dante
works.title: The Divine Comedy
works.copy: The Modern Library volume reprinted the prose translation that J. M. Dent of London published in three volumes of its Temple Classics series (1899–1901): the *Inferno* by John Aitken Carlyle, the *Purgatorio* by Thomas Okey and the *Paradiso* by Philip Wicksteed. That translation is printed here. Donald Pearce, who took the course, names it as the version in which the cantos were to be written out from memory. The text is taken from the Temple volumes. This site found no scan of the Modern Library reprint that is free to read online, so it has not checked whether the reprint altered any wording. The *Inferno* is Carlyle’s translation in its second edition of 1867, with about two hundred alterations by the Temple editor, Hermann Oelsner, which are in square brackets. Longfellow’s verse translation and the Italian are printed here as well.

works.author: Horace
works.title: Odes
works.copy: The Loeb volume prints the Latin with C. E. Bennett’s prose translation of 1914 facing it. No text of Bennett’s translation that had been checked against the book was found, so John Conington’s verse translation is printed here with the Latin. It was first published in 1863, and the text is that of the third edition, of 1865. Conington left out four odes (I.25, II.5, III.20 and IV.10), which are printed here in Latin only.

works.author: Augustine
works.title: Confessions
works.copy: The Loeb volumes print William Watts’s translation of 1631. No text of it that had been checked against the book was found, so E. B. Pusey’s translation of 1838, which revises Watts, is printed here.

pieces.title: The Fox’s gold, song and sentence

works.author: Pascal
works.title: Pensées
works.copy: The Everyman volume is W. F. Trotter’s translation of 1904, which is printed here without T. S. Eliot’s introduction of 1931.

works.author: Racine
works.title: Phèdre
works.copy: R. B. Boswell’s verse translation of 1890 is printed here, under the title *Phaedra*.

works.author: Blake
works.title: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

works.author: Goethe
works.title: Faust, Part I
works.copy: The Everyman volume is Albert Latham’s translation of 1908. No text of it that had been checked against the book was found, so Bayard Taylor’s translation of 1870 is printed here.

works.author: Kierkegaard
works.title: Fear and Trembling
works.copy: No complete translation that is out of copyright was found. L. M. Hollander’s selection of 1923, about a third of the book, is printed here.
works.borrow: For the whole book, Walter Lowrie’s translation of 1941 can be [borrowed from the Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/feartremblingdia0000skie_r6e3) with a free account.

works.author: Baudelaire
works.title: Intimate Journals
works.copy: The Random House volume of 1930 is Christopher Isherwood’s translation, with an introduction by T. S. Eliot. No free text of it was found, so Joseph Shipley’s translation of 1919 is printed here. Shipley calls the book *Intimate Papers* and its two journals *Rockets* and *My Heart Laid Bare*. He leaves out some pages of each.
works.borrow: A later edition of Isherwood’s translation (Marcel Rodd, 1947), which has an introduction by Auden, can be [borrowed from the Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/intimatejournals0000char_k2x1) with a free account.

works.author: Ibsen
works.title: Peer Gynt
works.copy: The Everyman volume is R. Farquharson Sharp’s translation of 1921. No text of it that had been checked against the book was found, so the translation by William and Charles Archer is printed here. It was first published in 1892, and the text is the one they revised in 1907.

works.author: Dostoevsky
works.title: The Brothers Karamazov
works.copy: The Modern Library volume is Constance Garnett’s translation of 1912, which is printed here.

works.author: Rimbaud
works.title: Une Saison en Enfer
works.set: translated by Delmore Schwartz, New Directions
works.copy: Schwartz’s translation of 1939 is in copyright. The translation printed here appeared unsigned in *The Dial*, an American magazine, in July 1920 under the title *A Season in Hell*. It is attributed to J. S. Watson, Jr., one of the magazine’s owners. In the chapter “Alchemy of the Word” Rimbaud quotes seven of his own poems, and the translation leaves them in French. The French text of 1873 is printed with it.

works.author: Rilke
works.title: The Journal of My Other Self
works.copy: The list names the edition that W. W. Norton published in 1930 under this title. Its translators were M. D. Herter Norton and John Linton, and their translation is printed here. The book is now called *The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge*.

texts.label: Norton and Linton
texts.translator: M. D. Herter Norton and John Linton

works.author: Kafka
works.title: The Castle
works.copy: The Knopf volume of 1930 is the translation by Willa and Edwin Muir, which is printed here.

works.author: T. S. Eliot
works.title: The Family Reunion
works.copy: In copyright in the United States until 2035. It can be [borrowed from the Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/familyreunionpla00elio) with a free account.

works.author: Gluck
works.title: Orpheus
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s Italian and English libretto, translated by Manfredo Maggioni. The libretto is headed *Orpheus and Eurydice*.

record.title: “Che farò senza Euridice,” from the last act of Gluck’s *Orpheus*
record.performers: Sigrid Onegin, contralto, with orchestra. Brunswick record 50039, made about 1922. Four minutes.
record.credit: A collector’s transfer from the disc, at the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/sigrid-onegin-christoph-willibald-gluck-orfeo-ed-euridice-che-faro-senza-euridice-brunswick-50039).

works.author: Mozart
works.title: Don Giovanni
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s Italian and English libretto, which calls the opera *Don Juan*. It stops before the last scene of the opera.

record.title: “Là ci darem la mano,” the duet of Don Giovanni and Zerlina in the first act of Mozart’s *Don Giovanni*
record.performers: Geraldine Farrar, soprano, and Antonio Scotti, baritone, with orchestra. A Victor record made on October 4, 1909. Three minutes.
record.credit: Transfer by the Library of Congress, in its [National Jukebox](https://www.loc.gov/item/jukebox-125909/).

works.author: Mozart
works.title: The Magic Flute
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s Italian and English libretto. It follows the Italian version of the opera, in which the spoken scenes of the German original are cut or sung.

record.title: “Der Hölle Rache,” the Queen of the Night’s aria in the second act of Mozart’s *The Magic Flute*
record.performers: Frieda Hempel, soprano, with orchestra. A Gramophone Company record made on September 12, 1911. Three minutes.
record.credit: A collector’s transfer from a later pressing of the disc, at the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/der-holle-rache-db-365).

works.author: Beethoven
works.title: Fidelio
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s German and English libretto.

record.title: “Abscheulicher! Wo eilst du hin?”, Leonore’s scene in the first act of Beethoven’s *Fidelio*
record.performers: Frida Leider, soprano, with orchestra. Both sides of a Polydor record of the early 1920s. Seven and a half minutes.
record.credit: A collector’s transfer from the disc, at the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/78_abscheulicherwoeilstduhin_191_03).

works.author: Wagner
works.title: The Flying Dutchman
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s German and English libretto.

record.title: Senta’s ballad, from the second act of Wagner’s *The Flying Dutchman*
record.performers: Maria Jeritza, soprano, with orchestra. Victor record 74776, made in 1922. Four and a half minutes.

works.author: Wagner
works.title: Tristan und Isolde
works.copy: The English version by H. and F. Corder, from the libretto published by Oliver Ditson of Boston, which does not credit them. The libretto is headed *Tristan and Isolda*.

record.title: Isolde’s last song, the “Liebestod,” which ends Wagner’s *Tristan und Isolde*
record.performers: Johanna Gadski, soprano, with orchestra conducted by Walter B. Rogers. Victor record 88058, made on June 16, 1915. Four minutes.
record.credit: Transfer by the Library of Congress, in its [National Jukebox](https://www.loc.gov/item/jukebox-124612/).

works.author: Wagner
works.title: Götterdämmerung
works.copy: Margaret Armour’s translation of 1911, *The Twilight of the Gods*.

record.title: Siegfried’s Funeral March, from the last act of Wagner’s *Götterdämmerung*
record.performers: The Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. Both sides of His Master’s Voice record D 502, made in 1920. Eight minutes.
record.credit: Transfers by the Centre for the History and Analysis of Recorded Music, King’s College London, at the Internet Archive: [the first side](https://archive.org/details/78_siegfrieds-funeral-march-part-1-gtterdmmerung_royal-albert-hall-orchestra) and [the second](https://archive.org/details/78_siegfrieds-funeral-march-part-2-gtterdmmerung_royal-albert-hall-orchestra).

works.author: Bizet
works.title: Carmen
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s French and English libretto of about 1910. It follows the version of the opera in which the scenes that were spoken at the first performance are sung.

record.title: The Habanera, from the first act of Bizet’s *Carmen*
record.performers: Geraldine Farrar, soprano, with orchestra conducted by Walter B. Rogers. Victor record 87210, made on December 9, 1914. Three minutes.
record.credit: Transfer by the Library of Congress, in its [National Jukebox](https://www.loc.gov/item/jukebox-11761/).

works.author: Verdi
works.title: La Traviata
works.copy: The English version from Rullman’s Italian and English libretto, which calls the opera *The Lost One*.

record.title: “Sempre libera,” which ends the first act of Verdi’s *La Traviata*
record.performers: Amelita Galli-Curci, soprano, with orchestra. Victor record 64820, made on March 7, 1919. Under three minutes. To judge by old librettos, six of the eight lines as she sings them have other words than the libretto printed here.
